extracted.intended_audience: practitioners and students of early metallurgy, lapidary work, and natural philosophy (alchemists, metallurgists, lapidaries)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical criteria for identifying, testing, refining, and classifying metals and gemstones (cupellation, amalgamation, tests of purity, gem luster/hardness/transparency, provenance and purported virtues) drawn from a historical treatise on metals and stones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of transmutation
rubrics_metrics.description: Czterüm quod ad alia artinet metalla; tranfmutari nequeunt ig aurüum, neque argentum: nam metalla illa exufla (sic) exufa fünt; quod exuflum eft, non potett amplius redire ad priftinam puritatem. — i.e., metals generally cannot be truly transmuted into gold or silver; gold is 'perfect' and other metals cannot attain its proper nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains philosophical/empirical limit: while color or weight may be altered by artifices, essential qualities (the species/nature) of gold and silver are not produced anew; only accidental changes occur. Use of fire/fluxes may change appearance but not create true aurum/argentum. Historical claims are discussed but treated skeptically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential distinguishing properties of gold and silver
rubrics_metrics.description: Aurum perfectum est; & specie differt ab aliis metallis; cum ignibus ex toto resistat. — gold distinguished by its perfection, resistance to fire, specific color, density and enduring firmness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To judge whether a metal is true gold: test resistance to fire (should not be consumed), observe color and specific gravity (density), and evaluate tenuitate (fineness) and firmitas (firmness). These are primary indicators of 'true' gold vs imperfect substitutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary observable changes claimed for conversion toward gold
rubrics_metrics.description: Vt veró argentum vivum in aurum tranímutetur, necesse est yt firmétor ignibusque resístat, & tingatur. — i.e., for silver/mercury compounds to approach aurum one must produce greater firmness, resistance to fire, and coloration toward gold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists empirical conditions often cited by practitioners who hoped to 'make' gold: increase density, alter color toward gold, remove 'pinguedo' (fatness) and render the metal more firm and refractory to fire. The text records reported experiments (e.g., Hydrargirion claims) but emphasizes that such changes are easier said than truly transmutative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests of metal purity by heating (ignis test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Argumentum: si aurum non est obnoxium ignibus (aurum ignibus resistit) — metals should be tested by fire to see whether they are consumed or lose properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat the metal and observe whether it is consumed, attenuated, changes color, or resists. Metals that remain and do not 'absumuntur' by fire are indicated as purer/nobler. Use repeated heating and comparison with known samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of silver by lead (cupellation) and use of lead as collector
rubrics_metrics.description: Plumbum used to collect and separate silver: 'cum plumbi substatia media fit inter propria ac fumi; argentia ... plumbum nigrum et ipsum absumitur igne ... inde argentum manet' — lead collects silver which is left after cupellation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: alloy or mix ore with lead, melt; upon heating the lead oxidizes and either forms a black lead that separates or is absorbed by the furnace, leaving silver behind. The text gives details on decantation, supernatant lead, and subsequent burning to remove lead (cupellation). Attention to the state (white/black lead) and repeated operations affect yield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aqua separationis (water/separation) method for argentum
rubrics_metrics.description: Argentum in aqua: 'aqua separationis vniuerfum colliquatur; cum confitet in ea aurum poni diffolug Neutro igitur modo inesse potest; sed exigua pars actui quae dum separari nequit...' — washing/dissolution can separate parts but a residue often remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use washing, dissolution (possibly in acidic media such as vinegar), and decantation to remove lighter impurities; recognize that some fraction remains not separable by simple aqueous treatment. Combine with heat or further fluxes if necessary; small portions may remain until different processes (ignis) act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mercury (argentum vivum) and amalgamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Argentum vivum (mercury) is similar to gold in weight/tenuity and used in attempts to approach gold: 'argentum viuüm auro proximius esse videtur quàm argento' and many used hydrargyrion techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mercury amalgamation is useful to collect and purify silver and to alter apparent properties; volatilization/sublimation and subsequent processing may produce powders/pellets. The text records recipes and cautions that though mercury treatments change appearance and handling, they do not guarantee true transmutation into gold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refining/silvering and gilding recipes (practical operations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipes for producing silver/gilded surfaces: eg. mixing auripigment, salt (halinitrum), nitre, arsenic, vinegar, vinagre and repeated calcination and washing to obtain pulvis for treatment of silver/gilt objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical proportions are given (e.g., two pounds halinitrum to one pound something, mixing arsenic etc.), repeated washing, calcination under coals, and use of wine dregs. These are presented as tested artisanal techniques for producing silvering or gilding and for adulterating coinage (warning about misuse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and practical differences of lead and tin (plumbum/stannum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead species: 'plumbum nigrum' and 'plumbum album' differ in properties and uses; stannum (tin) likewise has particular characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify lead by color and behavior on heating; white lead behaves like tin and can be produced or adulterated; mixing lead of various sorts with copper or brass affects color, hardness and value. Use of particular lead types is recommended/avoided depending on desired product.

rubrics_metrics.name: General metallic evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Metals are to be evaluated by: color, ponderis (weight), tenuitate (fineness/tenuity), firmitate (firmness), and resistance to fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a metal sample, check color (true hue), specific gravity (weight), thinness/fineness (tenuitas), firmness (mechanical strength), and whether the metal resists consumption by fire. These combined indicate nobility/purity and proximity to gold/silver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metallic affinity and incompatibilities (amicitia/interdicta)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain metals 'amicitia' (friendship) or antipathy exists: 'inde etiam metallorü amicitia iam aurü-& argentü plum... amiciia' — e.g., lead mixes with copper/brass readily but is 'odious' to silver and gold which reject lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: in smelting and refining, some metals alloy easily while others repel; awareness of affinities informs which fluxes/alloys to use and how to separate contaminants (e.g., lead tends to separate and is removable from gold/silver by cupellation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and criteria distinguishing gemma from lapis
rubrics_metrics.description: Gemma defined as 'nitens, natura rarum atq; paruum' — a shining, rare, and small stone; not every shining stone (marmor etc.) qualifies as a gemma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To call a material a gem (gemma), require smallness/relative rarity and pronounced shine (nitor). Large shining stones (some marbles) are not termed gemma. Examples: pearls, corals, turquoise, oriental topaz are treated as gems when they meet these qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary gem-evaluation criteria: luster (nitor) and hardness (durities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Order of importance: nitor (luster) first, then durities (hardness), then opacitas/opacity or transparency, then color (diluted or intense). 'Cur reddant gemmz imaginem, est nitor primum, inde duritas, tertio opacitas, quarto color dilutus.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing gemstones, prioritize luster (how it fills the eye), then hardness (resistance to abrasion and durability), then whether it is transparent or opaque, and finally the purity/intensity of color. Polishing increases luster and may reveal other qualities; small blemishes are more visible in high-luster gems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency (perspicuitas) testing (immersion in water)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency test: Onychis speciem (onyx-like) becomes transparent when immersed in water; more generally, some gems' perspicuitas is revealed by immersion or polishing: 'His igitur de causis aqueus color ... vires convenit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To test a gem's transparency, place in water or polish and observe if light penetrates and image transmission/clarity improves. Transparent behavior in water is diagnostic for certain varieties; lack of perspicuitas despite polish suggests opacity or different classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix/origin as identification criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Many gems have a matrix (matricem) or are born in particular host stones: 'quz inter lapides generantur... habet unaquaeque gemma suam matricem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the host rock or matrix and locality; matrix association helps identify gem species (e.g., emeralds with prase, carbuncle in certain hosts). Provenance and matrix are useful for authentication and assessment of rarity/quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance and climate influence on gem quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Gems from hot regions tend to have the finest 'succo' (juice) and therefore greater luster and value; colder regions produce fewer noble gems: 'in calidis regionibus... succus ille fit tenuissimus.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider geographic origin: gems from particular regions (Orient, Bohemia, etc.) are historically valued differently. Use provenance together with physical tests to judge quality rather than relying solely on local reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of alleged virtues and uses of gems
rubrics_metrics.description: Many gems are ascribed medicinal or protective virtues (e.g., hyacinthus protects from lightning, calms spirit, useful against fear; ring-worn gems may be more efficacious than loose stones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report and weigh traditional authorities (e.g., Galen, Albertus) and empirical testimony when attributing virtues. Note placement matters (ring vs pendant) and that some claims are anecdotal or legendary; practitioners should prefer repeated observation and authoritative testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of gem setting/wear position on efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A gem worn on a ring or near the tongue is considered more effective: 'in annulo geftata gemma, vel collo appensa quod modo validius est; aut eam sub lingua retenta quod ...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prescribing gem use for virtue/therapy, consider that wearing a gem in direct contact (ring, under tongue) or on the person may strengthen its supposed effects; authors caution that authority and ritual also influence perceived efficacy.
